Show, list and copy table styles

Source: R/tables.R
jstyle.Rd

A style holds a table's look and a journal's or a report's conventions: the font, the caption's form, the rules, the decimals, and for each table type its columns and labels. jstyle() lists the styles jstats can find; jstyle("myjournal") checks a style file and prints every setting the style gives, marking each one it takes from another style; and jstyle("apa", save.as = "myjournal") saves a copy as a style file, myjournal.jstyle, every setting written out with a note on what it does and what it takes, to edit in any text editor (the step SPSS calls "Save TableLook As"). jstyle("myjournal", open = TRUE) opens the file in the editor instead of printing it.

Usage

jstyle(style = NULL, save.as = NULL, overwrite = FALSE, open = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

style

The style's name in quotes – "apa", "report" or a style file's – or a path to a style file; NULL (the default) lists the styles, or with save.as or open copies or opens joptions(style = ).

save.as

A name for the copy, in quotes: written as <name>.jstyle in the style folder when one is set, else in your jstats folder (tools::R_user_dir("jstats")), or to a path given with a folder. "apa" and "report" name the built-in styles, so neither can be a copy's name; a file named apa.jstyle or report.jstyle is not read, and jstats says so.

overwrite

Logical. Replace a style file that exists? With FALSE (the default) an interactive session asks, and one that cannot ask stops.

open

Logical. TRUE opens the style's file in the editor, as base R's file.edit() does (in RStudio, a tab beside your script), and prints no settings; the file is still checked, and a value it cannot use is named. With save.as it opens the file just written. Only in an interactive session: a script opens nothing. The built-in styles have no file; save a copy to open one.

...

Settings for a short copy, with save.as: a general setting by its name (font = "Arial"), a table type's settings in a list named for its section (regression = list(fit.rows = "r2")). jstyle_settings lists them all. Any other input stops with "unused input".

Value

Invisibly: the styles found (a data frame of name and path), the style, or the path of the file written.

Details

jstats has two built-in styles: "apa", APA 7's conventions for a journal, and "report", the plain look the report style manuals share – Arial 10, "Table 1:" and the title on one line, a light grey header, an upright "Note:" – based on apa. A style for an agency or an institute is a copy of report with its own colors and font.

Given settings, jstyle(save.as =) writes a short file instead: the style it copies named on its based.on line, and only the settings given, which is all a small change needs. A general setting is given by its name; a table type's settings go in a list named for its section: jstyle("apa", save.as = "myapa", font = "Arial", regression = list(fit.rows = c("r2", "n"))). A short file takes everything else from its base, so it travels with it: a file based on a style of your own works on another computer, or from another folder, only where that style can be found too. A base given by its path is written by its path, which is where jstats finds it; a base given by its name is looked for in the folders below.

A style file is plain text: a setting is a name, an equals sign and a value; a # starts a note; the general settings come first, then one section per table type, [descriptives], [frequencies], [regression], [logistic], [correlation], [ttest], [anova], [crosstab], [reliability] and [multiresponse]. A setting the file leaves out comes from the style its based.on line names. jstyle_settings lists every setting and what it takes. jstats looks for a style named in a call in the style folder (joptions(style.dir = )), the working directory and your jstats folder, in that order.

Making a style with an AI assistant

A style file is plain text, so an AI assistant can write one from an example report. Give it a complete copy, which lists every setting and what each takes – jstyle("report", save.as = "myagency") writes one; a short file hides the settings it takes from its base – and the example, with a request such as:


Attached are myagency.jstyle, a jstats table style whose notes say what
each setting does and what it takes, and Report.pdf. Rewrite the style
file so that jstats tables look like the tables in the report, following
the instructions at the top of the file, and list what the settings
cannot reproduce.

Save its reply over the file and run jstyle("myagency"), which names any value it cannot use (give that back to the assistant), then try the style: jtable(c1, style = "myagency", open = TRUE). An assistant can reach only the looks the settings make; it is told to say what it could not reproduce rather than invent a setting.

See also

jtable for the tables, jstyle_settings for every setting a style holds.

Examples

# The styles jstats can find, and the folders it looks in
jstyle()
#> Styles
#>   apa     built into jstats (the default)
#>   report  built into jstats
#> 
#> jstats looks for a style file in these folders, in this order:
#>   /home/runner/work/jstats/jstats/docs/reference (the working directory)
#>   /home/runner/.local/share/R/jstats (your jstats folder, not created yet)
#> 

# Every setting of the built-in styles
jstyle("apa")

#> Style written to /tmp/RtmpLJH66q/myjournal.jstyle
#> 
jstyle("apa", save.as = file.path(tempdir(), "myapa"), overwrite = TRUE,
       font = "Arial", regression = list(fit.rows = c("r2", "n")))
